text: When health insurance companies deny claims and appeal is not very likely. Federal data shows that companies issued more than 49 million denials in 2021, but customers appealed only about two tenths of 1% of them. And while some denials come with specific justifications, most explanations are vague. Ali Rogan explores how at least one major health insurance company is using artificial intelligence to assess and often deny claims in bulk. Investigative journalists at the nonprofit ProPublica found that the health insurance company SIGDA uses an automated system that allows it to instantly reject claims on medical grounds without even opening the customer's file. Some are accusing SIGNA of using the system to help cut costs at the expense of the patients, a claim which SIGNA denies. Joining me now is my amiller, one of the reporters who worked on the story. But thank you so much for joining us. Can you explain to me how this system works? Yeah, absolutely. When you go to a doctor or, you know, see your health air provider, they'll send in a claim to your health insurance plan. And they'll list the diagnosis that think that you have and then a list of test procedures that they want to run. We learned that there's a process that was developed at SIGNA about a decade or so ago in which they created this code, this computer code, this algorithm, that says we're going to prove them if they match certain conditions. But if they don't match another condition, let's say a diagnosis that they don't have to think that is worthy of that treatment. Then it will be sent to the desk of a medical director, which is a company doctor. And that health that doctor is going to be able to quickly sign off on rejecting that claim and saying we're not going to cover it. In two months last year that happened on average of under two seconds. So these medical directors were essentially saying for, you know, 50 patients at a time they wouldn't even open a patient file. But they were signing their name off and saying, actually this claim is not medically necessary. And so we're not going to cover it. Now I want to read to you from a statement that SIGNA has provided. First they say that this automated process allows us to pay providers for claims quickly and automatically and allows medical directors time to look at more complex reviews. It also says that even a denial should not result in any additional out of pocket costs for patients who are using in network providers. What did you find related to those two statements that SIGNA makes? Yes. So on the first statement, it's true that some of the claims that are processed through the system, which is called PXDX. If they match the diagnoses and the treatments on the list, if the code sees that there's a match there, they will be automatically approved. However, then there's a batch of them that get automatically denied. And that's really what we're focusing on on the story is the batch of claims, which we found in two months last year, exceeded 300,000 claims. So it's not an insignificant amount. And to the second point about, you know, that this shouldn't result in any out-of-pocket cost for patients. Unfortunately, the reality is is oftentimes when we go to a doctor and nurse or to see a health care provider, we often have to sign off on a form. And in that form, we're saying that we'll take responsibility, financial responsibility for this outcome of this care. And so it does often get shunted onto the patient. And what kind of procedures are we talking about that are getting routinely denied? Yes. So unfortunately, we were trying to look for a comprehensive list of all of these claims that processed through the system. And we know that not all of the claims that SIGNA has end up going through the system. But of those that do we learn that vitamin D testing is labeled as part of the system. We learn that autonomic nervous system testing to test whether your nerves are working well. If you oftentimes, if you have diabetes or other autoimmune disease, you can have some nerve damage. Your fingers are your toes and so testing to kind of figure that out among other conditions. And fortunately, we could not find a comprehensive list of all of the different procedures that are tagged for the system. But those were two that we were able to conclude from our reporting. SIGNA and all insurers frankly in claims denial issues will say, well, there's always the appeal process. What does that look like in reality? Yeah, so one in seven claims are denied across the country and health insurance claims. So if effects a lot of people and yet one study found that 0.1% of all people who experience those denials actually took it to a step to do a formal appeal. When you're going about your day to day, maybe you're facing an illness or you're, you know, facing a disease, a chronic disease. It's hard to find the time and wherewithal to be able to figure out how to appeal these claims and the reality is that very few people do. And you know, we actually found through a reporting that SIGNA had a presentation in which they were putting forward the idea to put autonomic nervous system testing through the system. And in the cost benefit analysis, assessing whether to do this, they assumed only 5% of patients would end up appealing this. And that was part of the calculation of whether to put this test into this process or program or to leave it out. Now SIGNA is not the only insurer with some kind of automated system like exactly like this. Do you have a sense of how prevalent automated systems are right now in the health system writ large? It appears to be pretty prevalent and you know insurance companies are dealing with millions and millions of claims. And so in order to stand top of those and to maintain efficiency, which is what they've said. They've, you know, turned to these algorithms and computer coding programs to be able to process claims as quickly and efficiently as they as possible is what they say. So it seems that this kind of technology is pretty prevalent across the industry, although we're still reporting that out for other insurance plans and trying to confirm that. But yeah, it seems like it's pretty pervasive. Lastly, my other was a robust debate happening about the hazards of using AI where does this conversation fit into the broader debate about the utility and the hazards of using artificial intelligence. Yeah, and that's a great question and one that we're actually, you know, posing to regulators right now. Former insurance commissioner of California, Dave Jones was telling us that, you know, in the statutes, you need to have a thorough fair and objective assessment of these patient claims. And he was saying that if an insurer, if a medical director or a company doctor for an insurance plan is really looking at a claim in less than two seconds in an average of less than two seconds, can you achieve that results. Yeah, I'd pose that question really to the to the lawmakers regulators and to see, you know, where they would stand on that. My amiller with probably go, thank you so much for your time. Thanks for having me.
